Extract Ui class; convert Stuart to instance-based
commitResults.messageBody:
Moves all direct user I/O — the banner (including its RGB animation),
reading commands from stdin, and the reply()/divider-formatting logic —
out of Stuart into a new Ui class. Stuart no longer talks to
System.in/System.out directly; it goes through a Ui instance instead.

This required converting Stuart from a class of only static methods
into an instance-based one (private Ui ui field, public run() method,
main() reduced to `new Stuart().run()`), since nearly every method in
the old Stuart called the static reply() helper directly. Without this
change, extracting Ui would have meant threading a Ui parameter through
most of Stuart's private methods instead of letting them share one
instance field — the instance-based shape matches the target design's
own Duke(String filePath) / run() example.

TEXT_INDENT moved to Ui as a public constant (Ui.TEXT_INDENT), since two
of Stuart's error messages build their own indented continuation line
before ever reaching reply() and need the same indentation value.

No behavior change: verified via text-ui-test that console output is
byte-identical across all three test scenarios (write, load, corrupted
load) before and after this refactor.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Storage class for loading/saving tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Moves DATA_FILE_PATH, loadTasks/saveTasks/parseSavedTask out of Stuart
into a new Storage class, constructed with the file path (matching the
target design's Storage(filePath) shape). Stuart's constructor now
takes filePath too, passed through from main(), instead of reading a
private constant directly.

Storage.load() throws StuartException only for a total read failure
(the file exists but can't be opened/read at all) - Stuart catches this
in run() and falls back to an empty task list, mirroring the target's
own try { tasks = new TaskList(storage.load()); } catch (...) pattern.
A single corrupted *line* is a different, non-fatal case: Storage still
tolerates it internally and reports it via the Ui passed into load()/
save(), so one bad line doesn't cost every other saved task, preserving
existing tested behavior.

Design trade-off worth noting: Storage.load()/save() both take a Ui
parameter so they can report warnings without Stuart having to inspect
their result first. This is a small, deliberate coupling to Ui rather
than a violation of separation of concerns - Storage's job (file I/O)
stays untouched by this; it just has a channel to report problems as
they occur, the same way a logger would.

Storage also has its own small, private parseDate() duplicating
Stuart's - the actual parsing is identical, but the error messages
differ on purpose: a user-typed date gets format guidance ("Please use
yyyy-MM-dd, e.g. ...") since they can fix it immediately, while a
corrupted saved date doesn't, since it's reporting a fact about old
data, not prompting a retry.

No behavior change: verified via text-ui-test that console output is
byte-identical across all three test scenarios (write, load, corrupted
load) before and after this refactor.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList class for the task collection
commitResults.messageBody:
Wraps the raw ArrayList<Task> that Stuart used to hold and manipulate
directly into a new TaskList, exposing add/delete/get/size and a
read-only getAll() (via Collections.unmodifiableList) instead of the
underlying mutable list. TaskList validates its own indices now:
get()/delete() throw StuartException("That's not a valid task
number.") for an out-of-range index, so the isValidIndex() check that
used to guard every mark/unmark/delete branch in Stuart is gone -
callers just call get()/delete() and let the existing catch
(StuartException) in the command loop handle a bad number, same as
every other user-facing error already does.

Storage.save()'s parameter widened from ArrayList<Task> to List<Task>,
since TaskList.getAll() returns the interface type, not the concrete
ArrayList - Stuart now passes tasks.getAll() directly.

One thing I deliberately did NOT copy from the target's own example:
its Duke(String filePath) constructor builds the TaskList from
storage.load() right there, before run() ever shows the banner. I
tried that first and it moved the "skipping a corrupted saved task"
warnings to print before the banner instead of after - a real,
unintended behavior change caught by text-ui-test failing. The target
snippet's run() body is just "//...", so it doesn't actually mandate
that ordering; I kept the load happening inside run(), after the
banner and greeting, exactly where it already was. tasks is therefore
a non-final field, reassigned once after loading, rather than set in
the constructor.

No behavior change: verified via text-ui-test that console output is
byte-identical across all three test scenarios (write, load, corrupted
load) before and after this refactor - after fixing the ordering
regression above, which the suite caught on the first run.

Moves the pure text-interpretation logic out of Stuart into a new
Parser class: parseIndex, parseDate, checkNoSaveDelimiter, and the
/by /from /to field-splitting for deadline/event commands (now
DeadlineFields/EventFields records instead of loose local variables).
Parser's job is turning raw command text into structured pieces, or
throwing StuartException if the *structure* is wrong (e.g. no "/by" at
all); it does not decide what happens next.

Deliberately NOT done in this step: run()'s if/else-if command dispatch
is untouched. Restructuring that around whatever Parser returns is a
separate, larger, riskier change - this step only relocates the string
parsing, so it could be verified byte-for-byte against the existing
test suite without also having to reason about a changed control flow
at the same time.

Content validation (is the description/date actually non-empty?) and
task construction stay in Stuart - Parser reports the shape of what was
typed, Stuart decides whether that content makes sense and what task to
build from it.

No behavior change: verified via text-ui-test that console output is
byte-identical across all three test scenarios (write, load, corrupted
load), including every existing malformed-deadline/event negative case.

Completes the Parser extraction: Parser.parseCommand(String) now
recognizes which command a line of input is (matching the same
keyword/prefix rules as before) and returns a ParsedCommand(type,
arguments) record. Stuart.run() switches on CommandType instead of an
if/else-if chain checking string prefixes directly - the keyword
recognition itself (equals/startsWith checks, stripping the keyword
off) has moved into Parser, alongside the field-parsing it already did.

Went with this lighter-weight approach rather than a full Command
object per type (each with its own execute() method) - one enum plus
one record is far less ceremony than ~9 small classes, at the cost of
Stuart's switch needing a case per command instead of dispatch being
implicit in which Command subtype got returned. For a command set this
size, the extra classes felt like more structure than the problem
needed.

Mechanical notes:
- The while loop is now labelled (readLoop:) so the BYE case's `break
  readLoop;` can exit the loop from inside the switch - a plain `break`
  there would only exit the switch statement.
- Collapsed `String command = ui.readCommand(); String trimmedCommand
  = command.trim();` to one line - `command` was never used
  unstrimmed, a leftover from before this refactor started.
- MARK/UNMARK/DELETE's arguments are intentionally NOT trimmed by
  parseCommand (Parser.parseIndex already trims internally), matching
  exactly what the old inline substring() calls produced.

No behavior change: verified via text-ui-test that console output is
byte-identical across all three test scenarios (write, load, corrupted
load), including bye/list/sorted/on and every existing error case.
